Mr. Speaker, the debate so far has brought to the attention of parliament, rather forcibly, I believe, the fact that there is definitely a recession in our economic situation. We sometimes refer to this as a depression, but I have found that people occasionally take offence when we speak of a depression. They seem to think that "recession" is a more polite term for the situation. I do not know that there is any difference. As an hon. member pointed out in the past, a recession is when your neighbour loses his job, but when you lose your job it is a depression. We are somewhere in between those two definitions.
It has become abundantly clear that there has been a serious falling off in agricultural income. Unemployment is higher than it was at this time last year, and retail trade has been falling off. This is a natural consequence of the first two factors.
This evening I am not going to go into the question of unemployment to any extent, because my colleagues will deal with that


much more thoroughly than I could; but I should like to devote a little time to the question of an agricultural policy for Canada. I am glad that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in his seat tonight, because most of what I shall have to say will refer to his department as well as to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
First of all I should like to say that I believe every member of this house subscribes to the proposition which has been stated here and elsewhere so often by members of all parties that agriculture is entitled to its fair share of the national income. What I have to propose will not be in the nature of asking this parliament to hand out anything or to give preferred treatment to this basic industry which perhaps of all industries in Canada deserves preferred treatment. Rather my object will be to outline a policy which will, as near as it is possible to do so, bring to agriculture its fair share of the national income.
I should like to begin by quoting a resolution passed at a recent convention of the Manitoba farmers' union. A number of resolutions were passed dealing with agriculture, all of them of some importance, but I believe this one is the hub of all the resolutions, perhaps the basic resolution. I quote:
Whereas the price of farm products and farm income is constantly dropping while farmers' cost of production is increasing and there are no signs of parity between what the farmers earn and what they must pay for what they buy, and agriculture has therefore reached a most unstable position in comparison with other industries;
Therefore be it resolved that we. the Manitoba farmers' union, strongly urge our federal government to establish a policy of forward pricing on all agricultural commodities, which would bear a 95 per cent parity relationship to other goods and services, thus bringing about stability in agriculture and strengthen our whole economy.
I say that resolution is basic because if it were carried out it would involve the putting into effect of a number of supplementary policies which possibly would help to bring about the objective I have stated, that is a fair share of the national income to agriculture. Before I go on to outline the proposals I am going to make I want to say that I do not consider them to be either conclusive or exhaustive. I should like to hear proposals from all sides of the house so the government might summarize them, take from them what they believe to be constructive and practical and then come back to this house with a policy for agriculture which would bring about some stability and future for that great industry.
As part of that policy I should like to see a system of marketing boards. It is true that there are some marketing boards in existence.

In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred to one of them, the one which perhaps stands out above all others, the Canadian wheat board. This board has been one of the most successful in the history of marketing in this country. However, there are many other types of marketing boards needed if we are to attain that orderly marketing which I believe was the objective of all hon. members of this house in 1945 and the post-war years; at least hon. members from all sides of the house seemed to agree with that objective.
As one of the steps toward it I would suggest that every effort be made to assist those provinces which are now trying to organize livestock marketing boards. The Minister of Agriculture well knows that in the prairie provinces at least some definite steps have been taken. A great deal of planning has gone into the proposed establishment of marketing boards for livestock. In recent months other provinces have shown an interest in that project. As I read the press and according to what I hear from the agricultural organizations, the most recent development is the idea that if enough of the provinces show an interest in setting up livestock marketing boards, then the federal government can come to their assistance by co-ordinating their efforts through a national livestock marketing board and in that way establish a policy of orderly marketing from coast to coast. That is something that would also be necessary in connection with interprovincial and international trade in livestock and livestock products.
But perhaps the most important thing towards which the farm organizations are looking, so far as this house is concerned, is the establishment of floor prices for livestock products. Obviously it would be beyond the financial possibilities of any one province, and particularly of the prairie provinces whose revenue is very unstable as recent years have shown, to take the financial responsibility of establishing floor prices for livestock commodities within their own borders. The provinces can and no doubt will help in the organization, regulation and administration of livestock marketing boards within their own borders, but when it comes to the question of guaranteeing a floor under which the price will not be allowed to drop, it is only at the federal level that this financial responsibility can be carried. I hope that, as part of an over-all marketing policy, the government will consider helping the provincial farm organizations which have done a great deal of important preliminary spade work. A great deal of information has been elicited in connection with these boards.
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny The federal government can help them to co-ordinate their efforts through a national livestock marketing board.
I should also like the government and this house to give some attention to the proposal that has been made by various farm organizations of a two-price system for Canadian wheat. It has been proposed that on the domestic market-that is, for that portion of the wheat which is sold for Canadian consumption-a price should be set which should bear a relationship to other prices. It has been pointed out, and I think with some authenticity, that it would not be a departure from regular practices so far as business is concerned. I am informed that it is standard practice. The figures I am going to use were given to me. I have not checked them for accuracy. For example, as to the automobile industry, when they sell automobiles in Canada at wholesale for about $1,400 it is not unusual for them to offer those same automobiles in Europe for $700 and in some cases for less than that in countries like Australia and New Zealand.

speechtext: Have you any evidence to that effect?

speechtext:
I have just said that these figures were given to me and that I have not checked them for accuracy. If my hon. friend has evidence to the contrary, I should like to hear it. I will say this without any hesitation. It is the practice of Canadian manufacturers to offer their goods in other countries at prices lower than the prices at which they offer them in Canada. That is the price system which is used for the purpose of meeting competition. In other words the automobile industry as an example, because it enjoys a rather unusual degree of protection in this country, is in a position to sell its products in Canada at prices higher than those at which they are offered elsewhere.
Certainly there is every justification for the grain producers in Canada to request that *their product in Canada, for Canadian consumption, command a price which will bear a relationship to other commodity prices within this country. If it is necessary, as a matter of staying in the world market, to offer that same product at a slightly lower price elsewhere, then that is something that may have to be done. But there can be no real argument why the Canadian grain producer should have to offer his product in Canada, for domestic consumption, at a price less than it is worth in relation to other goods and services.
I should also like the government to take into consideration at an early date the question of an investigation into price spreads.

The Address

Mr. Zaplitny It is about 20 years-in fact it was a little more than 20 years ago-since there was carried ouit in Canada a price spreads investigation. It was one of the highlights, perhaps, of the economic history of this country. Those who have read the results of that investigation in the report, which is still available, have found a wealth of information. Not all the recommendations that emanated from the report were acted upon, it is true, perhaps because of the rather unfortunate time at which it was published. But the very fact that the price spreads investigation was made, and that it received fairly wide publicity in this country, had its beneficial effect by focusing the attention of the public and of this house on the exploitation, the unfair trade practices and the many other deficiencies in our economic and so-called competitive system. Almost 21 years have gone by, and I think it is high time a similar investigation was made, as thoroughly as it is humanly possible to make it, in order to find out and to let the public know just what is happening to our price system.
I have, for example, a few figures which I obtained from a farmer who took some time off this winter and studied the price spreads in three of the basic grains produced. This material has been carefully checked, and this was the result of his investigation. For example, taking wheat, he discovered that a bushel of top-grade Canadian wheat produced approximately 72-2 per cent of flour and that at current prices the farmer would receive, if you break that down into pounds, anywhere from 1J to 2J cents per pound for his wheat, depending on the grade, the time at which it was sold and so on. When that wheat is milled into flour, that flour immediately retails at a price of 5J cents a pound. Made into bread it immediately brings a price of 13 cents a pound. In other words 100 pounds of flour, which make 129 loaves of bread, would bring this result if it were sold at the regular price. For the bushel of wheat the farmer sold he would receive about 96 cents to $1.25, depending on the grade; but the bread made from that wheat would sell at $7.28.
Even allowing for processing, handling, storing, selling and all other costs involved, that indicates a terrific spread, and an inquiry should be made into it so the producer and the consumer may both know just where the consumer dollar is going and to what extent the producer is receiving the proceeds of his product.
Then he went on to deal with oats and he produced these figures. On the oat prices quoted the farmer may receive anywhere


from three-quarters of a cent to a cent for each pound of oats marketed, depending again on the grade and other factors. It is estimated that 55 [DOT] 3 per cent of the content of oats can be turned into what we call rolled oats which are sold for human consumption. That product immediately sells for 19 cents a pound. The farmer receives anywhere from 20 to 52 cents per bushel for his oats, but when they are turned into rolled oats they sell for $3.62 a bushel. This is an enormous spread, and even making allowance for all necessary costs it gives rise to doubts as to whether it is normal procedure.
Then we come to barley, and on the basis of prices as they were at that time it was found that the farmer receives from 50 to 92 cents a bushel for his barley. It is estimated that about 36 pounds of dry malt can be made out of approximately 42 pounds of barley. Immediately the dry malt is worth 12 cents a pound, or a bushel of dry malt would be worth $4.32. If it is turned into liquid malt it is worth $9 instead of $4.32.

speechtext: How much of that is taxes?

speechtext:
Someone says, "How much of that is taxes?" As I have said, we have to make allowance for all costs that enter into the transaction and we would certainly make allowance for taxes. But having made these allowances, I still think it is a matter which needs some investigation. These figures deal only with three of the grains that are produced. The same thing can be said of a great many other products which seem to become unduly inflated in price somewhere along the line between the time they leave the hands of the producer and the time the consumer receives the benefit of them. I believe it would serve a useful purpose to have a full-scale inquiry into the costs of handling, selling and processing. In other words, we should find out what makes up the price spread between the producer and the consumer. If it is found that there are undue price spreads or that there is undue exploitation, then steps can be taken to correct the situation. I think that in itself would be of great benefit to the producer.
Then there is the question of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. When I saw on the order paper that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was introducing a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act I hoped that it would be something fairly comprehensive. I now find that it is a minor amendment. Perhaps the minister has in mind bringing in another bill later this session. Certainly it is time something should be done to accede to the joint request of the

four western provinces. As the Minister of Agriculture well knows, as recently as last year the ministers of agriculture of those provinces had a conference and made a joint request to have the operations of the act extended to cover all agricultural areas in the four western provinces.
I do not want to weary the house by reciting the many difficulties that have been created in the prairie provinces by the last two unusually wet years. Most of us are already aware of them. The minister himself had occasion not many months ago to attend a farmers' meeting in a part of my province where I understood the farmers presented their problems most vividly and at great length. I believe it is time for a move to bring all agricultural areas of the four western provinces under the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
It is true that to date the operations under the act have been chiefly concerned with soil and water conservation and related matters; but I think it has been amply proved by experience that there are many other problems, such as drainage, which are getting to the point where they are beyond the capacity of these provinces to handle by themselves. I believe it would greatly assist the prairie farmers if the designated area under the act were extended so the federal Department of Agriculture could undertake the construction of dams, proper drainage systems and other related works which would not only protect land that is normally cultivated but could reclaim much of the land that has been put out of production in recent years due to wet weather.
As part of our agricultural policy I should also like to see the greatest possible effort made to remove trade restrictions. A great deal has been said in this debate about the necessity for international trade. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), replying to some of the proposals made by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe), had this to say as appears at page 32 of Hansard of yesterday:
Here we all feel that expanding trade is desirable. We feel that it is almost necessary to the prosperity of the Canadian people, but we do not feel that it would be by high tariffs that expanding trade could be achieved in this country.
I agree thoroughly with that statement, but it does not seem to lie well side by side with some of the actions taken by this very government. For example, only last year a bill was passed amending the Customs Act under which a very deliberate attempt was made to restrict imports coming into Canada. I believe that some of the recent difficulties which have arisen between the 50433-7i
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny United States and Canada in relation to trade-difficulties which made it necessary for three of our senior ministers to make a hurried trip to Washington not long ago, the results of which we still have to hear- have arisen by reason of the provocation caused by that very legislation.
That legislation was ostensibly brought into the house as a measure of assistance to the textile industry, which had complained that it was losing much of its trade because of the interference of cheaper goods coming in from other countries. But it became clear very early in the operation of that legislation that it was not particularly aimed at keeping out textile imports. It was an instrument used to raise arbitrarily the invoice value of any manufactured goods which in the opinion of the Minister of National Revenue were or could be considered to be unfair competition for Canadian goods of the same nature. The effect of that has been to create a great deal of uncertainty on both sides of the border. In fact, I would say almost on all sides because, although affecting the United States particularly, it has affected other countries as well. It has created a problem both for the Canadian importer and the United States exporter.
In the past, under the legislation which existed before the amendment, an importer could, by looking at the various tariff schedules of duties, calculate pretty closely what it was going to cost him to bring in goods from the United States. But since that amendment went through and since the Minister of National Revenue was given practically dictatorial powers to arbitrarily set the invoice price of goods which he deemed, in his wisdom, to be in unfair competition with Canadian goods, the Canadian importer as well as the United States exporter has been left in the most unenviable position of not knowing at any time what price they can quote. It has been left to the whim and fancy of the minister, his deputy or his deputy s deputy or some fifteenth assistant in the department to endorse the invoice. That is not a way in which we can promote trade relations with other countries.
I agree thoroughly with the Prime Minister when he said that expanding trade is not going to be accomplished by raising tariffs, but the effect of what the government has done under that legislation has been exactly the opposite, apparently, of what the Prime Minister himself advocated. I am looking forward, Mr. Speaker, to seeing this government change that legislation and go back to the normal procedure under which those who carry on trade may be able to read the act

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny and follow its implications with some accuracy, rather than be left to the whim or fancy of some official who may have his own ideas.
Now, having said that, I want at this point to say that in order to implement practically all the things I have so far discussed, it seems to me it would be necessary for this government to enter into a certain amount of economic planning. The other day my leader advocated economic planning for this country. It could be seen that hon. members in other parts of the house did not agree. It seems rather strange to me that successful business people, as well as many professional people, who enter into undertakings admitting very freely and very quickly that the greatest degree of planning is necessary in order to be successful, seem to take the opposite attitude when it comes to planning on a national level.
Surely if we are going to carry out those requests which have been made by members speaking from the opposition side of the house, to say nothing of the requests of members speaking from the government side, certainly that will involve economic planning. I believe it should be accepted by this house as an economic fact that in the times in Which we live, our problems in the immediate future are not going to be lessened by the fact that we are entering each day farther and farther into the field of technological development and discovery.
The other day I read an article in Maclean's magazine, as no doubt many of you did also, dealing with atomic development in Canada. I was astounded, even though I thought I had been following atomic developments in this country fairly closely, to learn how much quiet and unpublicized progress had been made in that field, not only here but in the United States as well. This is true to perhaps an even greater degree in Great Britain, where it is now within the realm of possibility that atomic energy can be used as a source of power for vehicles and in many other ways. We are now entering into a field which could create another industrial revolution in Canada, yet there are those who suggest that we go blindly into that situation without any economic planning at all. They say, leave it to free enterprise.
I am not opposed to free enterprise, and I do not believe anybody in this house really is, within the field in which it can make its greatest contribution. But if this nation has any foresight and vision and wants to take advantage of the latest developments, discoveries and techniques, then certainly we should not make a fetish out of free enterprise and deny ourselves the benefits that can accrue from a little national planning.


In this respect, I should like to refer to a speech made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), who happened to pay our province a visit last year at the time of the by-election -I beg your pardon; I meant the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill). I was referring to him by his former portfolio; perhaps I liked him better in that portfolio.
In any event, he took part in the by-election in Manitoba and in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 6, 1954, is reported as having said:
The phrase "private enterprise" was a "Tory trademark" and Liberals should never use it.
Then he went on to say:
Private enterprise and public enterprise were both good, "and this country needs a lot o f them."
It is this second paragraph with which I agree quite thoroughly. I am not going to comment on the first one because I do not want to enter into a dispute as to who owns the trade mark "private enterprise". Perhaps the most interesting paragraph is the third one, in which he says:
But the trade mark of the party I belong to is human welfare and without working for this we do not deserve the power of office.
If one were to take those statements together, then I would be inclined to think that certainly at least a portion of the government is not sold altogether on what is commonly known as "private enterprise" and sometimes referred to as free enterprise. It appears that it was a good thing for him to be in rural Manitoba where we are a little more forward looking, perhaps, than some other parts of Canada, and the minister has come to the conclusion that perhaps a little public enterprise is a good thing for Canada too. I congratulate him on it.
As a matter of fact I pointed that out in my letter to the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press, and contrasted it with something that was said by the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) only a few days later. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration seemed to resent it. He apparently thought I was trying to take advantage of what he had said. He did admit in his reply to the newspaper that I did not misquote him. We did agree on that.
The point I am trying to make is this. I believe the old battle that has been going on for quite a long time in Canada as to which "enterprise" is the real enterprise is getting pretty well shopworn and out of date. Let us have enterprise; let us have national enterprise. Let some of it be private enterprise and some public enterprise. Let us not get bogged down in an argument trying to prove there is only one kind of enterprise

that can do anything in this country. Let the government, in order to carry out their policies, use the organized finances and the organized know-how which are available to it, and in co-operation with the provinces work out a system of developing our national resources that will provide the best possible form of social security. After all, that is the hallmark of civilization in any country.
Let us above all develop a certain amount of national pride in accomplishment, not in the narrow jingoistic sense that we feel we are better than any other people on earth, but a real, genuine love of the Canadian soil, an appreciation of the possibilities in our country and a full knowledge that we, as a nation, can go on to greater things regardless of whether they are done on the one hand through public enterprise or on the other hand through private enterprise, so long as they are done for the benefit of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I add my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Listening yesterday to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) and noting the ease with which he switched from his native tongue, French, to English, I thought of what I had noted in my first year in the House of Commons; that is, the innate courtesy of those who have been born to the French language. I wondered just how different the proceedings of the House of Commons would be if we, who have been born to the English language, were forced either by the rules or by courtesy to carry on the great bulk of our thinking and of our business in the house in a language different from that to which we were born. So may I add my sincere appreciation not only to the hon. member for Verdun but to all his compatriots in the House of Commons for their unfailing courtesy to us of another tongue.
I rise tonight to speak almost entirely on the question of war veterans allowances. I am not trying to gloss over the importance of unemployment in this country, because I do believe it is a serious matter. It is a matter about which every intelligent person in this whole country should feel deep concern, and I know that deep concern is felt most certainly by every member on this side of the house. However, I intend to reserve anything I have to say on that subject until we have before us the actual and final proposals of the government to deal with that particular question.
I want to speak tonight about war veterans allowances particularly because on the last
The Address-Mr. Philpott day I was here last spring I had to express in the most forthright terms of which I was capable my disappointment because we did not get at the last session of parliament an increase in the war veterans alowances along the general lines that had been recommended in the Canadian Legion brief, and which had been advocated in this house, as was so well pointed out by the gracious lady who decorates the house in more ways than one, namely the hon. member for Halton (Miss Bennett). She described how all members of all parties in the house had given her a thrill by standing up to advocate a fair deal for those people receiving war veterans allowances, and it certainly was an inspiration for me last year to see how party lines were forgotten.
I think the hon. member who had the honour of first speaking out on this subject was my very good and old friend, the smiling member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). And I know very well, as the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) said yesterday, that the veteran member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) waged a doughty battle on that subject last year. The same is true of members from all parties, including the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), as well as a great many members on this side of the house.
I was doubly thrilled because one of the reasons I had to leave the house a few days before the end of the last session was to go home to attend, shall we say, an indignation meeting of about six or seven hundred irate veterans-and irate veterans' wives, who are doubly irate-who were very much concerned about this matter of war veterans allowances and what they thought was an undue delay on the part of the government in giving them what they considered was their due. I had to do some very frank talking. I had to tell them that, so far as we on this side of the house were concerned-and I was sure it was also true of others in all parts of the house-we would continue to do our level best to see that those in Canada entitled to war veterans allowances got their just due at the earliest possible moment.
But I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been doubly thrilled by recent developments. During the summer months it became clear that the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) would not have available to him this year the comfortable surplus that has enabled this government to pay off over two billion dollars of our national debt in the last seven years. It became clear that for the first time in many years the minister would be faced with a deficit. In the light of these circumstances it gave me a double thrill to note that, notwithstanding these facts, the government yielded to the strong representations
102	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Philpott made to it from all sides of the house, and we are now assured that the war veterans of Canada are going to get their due by way of increased war veterans allowances and raised ceilings.
I am glad to see, too, that at last we have abandoned what I thought was a very foolish argument, namely that the war veterans allowance is just another type of old age pension. We know perfectly well that during the course of debate, when people are fighting for some great social reform, all sorts of arguments are advanced from all sides of the house, and they are advanced to achieve certain results. But it seems to me it would be a most unsound principle permanently to tie war veterans allowances to the general old age security and old age assistance scheme in Canada. Certainly if we believe in honouring our debts-and I believe every member in the house would honour his debts-we must look with great disfavour on any repudiation of any of the debts of Canada. And surely the debt we should honour most is the debt to our own war veterans, who bore the brunt for this country in time of need.
I received an extra thrill this year in seeing Canada step once again into the forefront in the matter of veterans' welfare legislation. It was one of my responsibilities this past summer, as I have no doubt it was the responsibility of many other members, to take up certain pension complaint cases with the British ministry of pensions. When I have had occasion to look into the British veterans' legislation I have been more impressed than ever with the fact that Canada's veterans welfare legislation is the finest in the world, and that we take second seat to none. And, due to the fact that it has received constant support from all sides of the house all down through the years, once again we take our position in the front rank in our treatment of those who stood in the front line for us in time of need.
This afternoon we had a little bit of advice from my good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about how we should talk to our Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe)'-if necessary, behind the curtains-if what was going to be done was not all we had hoped it would be. Well, of course, we have no way of knowing from the cabinet what is going to be done. I remember Lloyd George once said that there were never any cabinet secrets, because every cabinet minister he had ever known, except one, told the cabinet secrets to his wife, and the one exception told them to other men's wives. So it was suggested that the way to find out any cabinet secret


was to send your wife around to the v/ife of a cabinet minister, and you would soon find out what happened.
But I am afraid we have a very clammy lot in our cabinet. We cannot find out a single, solitary secret. But may I tell my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that, far from having to take the Minister of Veterans Affairs behind the curtains to prod him on to greater efforts for the war veterans of Canada, the shoe is very definitely on the other foot. When the time comes to reveal the story of the fight for fairness to the war veterans of Canada, far from having the present Minister of Veterans Affairs lag in that regard, we will find that he has been in the very front rank of the fight from first to last.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have had many great ministers of veterans affairs in this country from the days when we first got the war veterans allowance. We had that beloved dean of the house, the present hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), a great friend of the war veterans of Canada. Later on we had that great Scotsman, who stood up like a great highland granite mountain in his championship of the rights of the veterans of Canada. Still later we had our present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), who I sometimes think might even wish that he was back where he was before, but who takes second place to none in his steadfast championship of the rights of the veterans of Canada. May I say, Mr. Speaker, never within my knowledge or within my lifetime has there been a greater champion of the rights of the veterans of Canada than the present Minister of Veterans Affairs.
I think I am a pretty good-natured person. I was brought up in a family of 13 children, so I had to learn to be good-natured at a very early age and I hardly ever get really mad. But when I went home at one time this year I shall confess that I got really mad, and that was when some of my own compatriots from British Columbia said they were going to walk out of a certain convention because the Minister of Veterans Affairs had not championed the rights of the veterans with sufficient aggressiveness in the house. That really did burn me up, because I knew the true story of the fight he had waged at times when it was most difficult to wage it.
If you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. It is sometimes not an unmixed blessing to be the son of a very great personage. Sometimes when one is the son of a very great personage people are inclined to attribute his good qualities entirely to heredity. May I say that for my part, as one

who has long been concerned about the welfare of the veterans in Canada I honour the present Minister of Veterans Affairs because he is the son of a very great Liberal statesman; but may I say with even more emphasis that I honour the present Minister of Veterans Affairs because of his own personality and because of the fact that in the truest sense of the word he has won his own spurs without help from anyone.
May I just tidy up that part of my speech by saying that while I did go home last year feeling a very real disappointment because we had not been able to get through an increase in the war veterans allowance and the lifting of the ceiling at the last session, I feel douibly gratified now.
While I am passing out compliments, for just a minute may I offer an especial compliment to the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe), for his truly remarkable performance of yesterday. I must say that for very many years I have had a warm spot in my heart for the present Acting Leader of the Opposition, because I was born and brought up in the heart of old Tory Ontario, and I have a great, deep and abiding respect for a real, good old-fashioned Ontario Tory. I always know exactly where a real, good, old Ontario Tory stands; so I was not the least bit surprised yesterday when he gave this house that hour of, shall I say, education, mixed with amusement, because our friend the Acting Leader of the Opposition has that great attribute, that great quality of character. He is able to get us all laughing with him, and he is a big enough man to laugh with us all and at times even to laugh at himself and enjoy the laugh, and that is one of my measurements of a big man.
But much to my astonishment the piece de resistance of the speech of the Acting Leader of the Opposition came yesterday not, shall I say, in the characteristic form that one might expect from a good old-fashioned Ontario Tory, an expert on horses; it came in the form that I have been led to expect sometimes even in letters from my wife. I always find in letters from my wife there may be one or two pages; and then at the end there will be a p.s., and the whole thing she had to say in the letter was said in that last p.s. Therefore much to my astonishment yesterday, after I had listened to an hour of mixed enlightenment and amusement from the Acting Leader of the Opposition, I heard him read out the six points in the amendment to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. I found a real bombshell in point No. 6. Without any
The Address-Mr. Philpott notification whatsoever to the good old Conservative party of Canada the Acting Leader of the Opposition of the day committed his party, on the spur of the moment in the last point, point six, the p.s., to national health insurance. When I heard that my heart beat with joy, my cup of jubilation really ran over.
I remember Adlai Stevenson's witty wisecrack in the last election. He was talking about General Eisenhower attempting to drag the Republicans screaming into the twentieth century. The Acting Leader of the Opposition very clearly did not attempt to drag the Conservative party of Canada screaming into the second half of the twentieth century because he very astutely did not give them any advance notice of what was going to be in point six, or the p.s., of his amendment.
When I saw his remarkable feat of agility, for some reason or other I had to think of the last time I was at the circus. I thought our friend gave an even more remarkable performance than the high diver I saw there. When I went to the circus I saw the performer walk up to that little pint-sized swimming pool. He looked at the big ladder and started to climb it. He climbed hundreds of feet and stood on a little board and dived and came right down into the swimming pool.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Acting Leader of the Opposition gave an even more remarkable performance. He landed in the swimming pool with the whole Conservative party, but he did not climb the ladder and therefore no one had a chance to see what was coming off.
May I say also that when I heard the mixed laughter and cheers I felt just a wee bit sorry for my good friend the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) because he seemed to me for just a moment to be like one of those fellows who went to swim in English bay at Vancouver on New Year's day. As he was just about to take the plunge somebody got away with his swimming trunks and for a moment he was in a rather embarrassing predicament. So for a moment yesterday the leader of the C.C.F. party seemed to be in just a little bit of an embarrassing predicament for fear the Tories had at last got away with his swimming trunks, and he was not just quite sure how to proceed.
May I say without any attempt at being facetious or witty just how glad all of us are on this side of the house who have always believed in the principle of national health insurance and who also believe in the principle of "not swift nor slow to change but in its season to bring the law". May I express

The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser the true hope that the smiling, genial, and highly respected Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) will still be around when our Prime Minister rounds out the final blueprint which was laid down in 1919 by the great Mackenzie King and we finally wind up the finest welfare state on earth with a national health insurance scheme. I am quite sure that the day after the Prime Minister brings in our national health insurance scheme we will all be ready to give a share of the credit to the Acting Leader of the Opposition for having seen the light in 1955.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. M. Fraser (St. John's East):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first of all to avail myself of the opportunity of congratulating most heartily the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Carrick), the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure that all hon. members of the house were impressed with the excellence of their speeches. I believe you will agree with me that as long as young men of their calibre continue to offer themselves for election to this house, parliamentary democracy in Canada is assured.
I should like also to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister and the government upon the farsighted and comprehensive policies, both domestic and foreign, which they have outlined in the speech from the throne. First of all I should like to reflect for a moment or two upon some of the aspects of external policy there envisaged.
I am sure the house will agree that in the realm of external policy paramount importance must be attached to the government's decision to ask parliament to ratify the Paris and London agreements. I am well aware that these agreements are to come up for debate in about a week's time and many of us are looking forward to participating in that debate. However, I urge the great importance of these agreements as a reason why I cannot refrain from addressing myself to them to some extent this evening.
As the house knows, these agreements provide for the restoration of sovereignty to West Germany, for the rearming of West Germany, and for her inclusion in both the west European union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We are aware also that the chief architect of these agreements was Sir Anthony Eden, the British foreign secretary. When the EDC project collapsed as a result of the failure of the French national assembly to ratify the EDC treaty it was he who found a workable substitute. He found 'Mr. Philpott.]
it, as it were, in a wedding of the Brussels treaty with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I feel that the free world owes a great debt to his brilliant initiative and superb statesmanship.
Like every hon. member of the house, I am sure, I approach the subject of German rearmament with very mixed feelings. This is a subject which arouses in every one of us grave misgivings. I think we can understand only too well the attitude of France. We know that France rejected the EDC treaty and showed a great deal of reluctance to agree to the inclusion of Germany in NATO. This is readily understandable. As we know, France has suffered the humiliation of German occupation three times in the course of the last 80 years or so, and each of those occupations was more humiliating than the previous one. Yet the French national assembly has decided to ratify that treaty.
The choice with which we are faced is not, I think, between a Germany rearmed and a Germany disarmed. The real choice is between a Germany rearmed within an international framework of control as proposed in these agreements and a Germany rearmed without controls.
Along with other hon. members I am looking forward to the statement we shall hear from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he expounds these agreements to the house. We know we will find a great deal of assistance and guidance in that exposition and in the skill and knowledge which he has brought to this and other subjects, both here and abroad at international conferences where he has represented Canada with such distinction and has added great lustre to the prestige of this country.
I turn now to the internal features of the speech from the throne. We are all much concerned with the problem of unemployment. Many speakers have referred to this serious situation, and I am glad to note that in the speech from the throne the government has put forward proposals to deal with this situation. I find in the speech from the throne a constructive and positive approach to that problem. It is a twofold approach.
First of all there is proposed an expanded public works program, designed to take up the slack in private industry. I note with satisfaction that it is the intention of the government to apply this program in all ten provinces. It will be welcomed in my own province of Newfoundland and in the riding of St. John's East, which I have the honour to represent. There, as in other constituencies right across this great country, there are

opportunities for the useful expenditure of public funds on practical objectives which will not only assist in coping with the problem of unemployment but will provide public works of permanent value to the communities concerned. There are several which I may suggest need to be attended to in my own riding of St. John's East. The federal departments in St. John's are seriously congested. Their present space is inadequate and there is an urgent need there for the construction of a new federal building to house the customs and various other departments. I would offer as a constructive suggestion that this might well form one of the projects of a public works program.
On an earlier occasion I referred in this house to the great need for an armoury at St. John's one which would be worthy of the great traditions and the splendid renown of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment, which traditions have been proudly maintained by the 59th regiment and the 166th regiment in the second world war and by the other fighting forces from Newfoundland.
I should also like to refer to the situation which at present exists at Torbay airport near St. John's. Torbay is the eastern terminal of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I regret to say that the terminal facilities there have become inadequate to cope with the growing volume of traffic which uses these facilities. There is need for enlargement of the terminal building, and in particular there is need for the inclusion in the plans of a canteen which will provide meals for passengers, many of whom arrive on flights at a late hour at night or in the early hours of the morning. The vagaries of climate in Newfoundland often lead to cancellation and postponement of flights, and this situation in turn aggravates the congestion of the terminal facilities at Torbay. There have been cases where passengers have not even had standing room in the terminal. I would therefore respectfully urge that attention be given to this matter. I am glad to note that it is the intention to proceed, as soon as possible in the spring, with the paving of the road connecting the provincial highway with the airport itself.
While I am on the subject of air facilities permit me to refer to the need for an air strip on Bell island. Bell island requires an air strip particularly in winter and early spring because it is frequently isolated then, by heavy seas and ice conditions, from Portugal Cove on the mainland of the Avalon peninsula. Moreover, an air strip on Bell island would form a most useful alternate for the terminal at Torbay in an emergency.
The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser
I should like to mention also the great advantages that would be derived from accepting the offer of the provincial government to establish the Signal Hill area at St. John's as a national historic park, but since this is the subject of a notice of motion which I have tabled I shall reserve my detailed remarks on that matter until later.
In my riding, as in all ridings in Newfoundland, there is need for marine works. I would refer particularly to the request which has been made to me for new wharves at Holyrood and Collier's. These are some of the fields in which, I think, the government would find opportunities to develop its policy of extension of public works projects and at the same time provide services of permanent usefulness to the communities in question. This is one angle from which the government proposes to deal with the problem of unemployment.
The other part of the approach, or the other line of main attack, is the proposal to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. Like all other members of the house, I heartily endorse this forward-looking measure. In doing so, may I be allowed to express the hope that when amendments are introduced to the Unemployment Insurance Act, its scope may be broadened sufficiently to include all classes of fishermen. Many of our fishermen in Newfoundland, and I expect in other provinces as well, are in a special category not only because their employment is so largely seasonal but partly because in Newfoundland, at any rate, so many of them are self-employed. As such they are not eligible under the present scheme, and the situation arises where those in one section of the population engaged in the fishing industry, namely those in the processing plants, are employed and receive wages while others, namely the men who go down to the sea in ships and face the hazards of wind and wave, are not eligible. Those are great hazards, as we have been reminded by two events very recently, the loss of the Newfoundland fishing vessel Student Prince and the terrible storms-the worst storms on record-which have been lashing the shores of Newfoundland for the last day or two, especially in my own riding of St. John's and many parts of Conception bay. I should like to take this opportunity to express my sincere sympathy to those who have lost valuable property in those heavy seas.
As I was saying, there is this unhappy contrast between those two classes engaged in the production of fish, namely those on land in the processing plants who are therefore eligible for unemployment insurance,

The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser and those fishermen who are self-employed and who go down to the sea and fish, and who are not eligible. That seems to me an anomaly which cries out for correction. I know it is a matter which is being given serious and sympathetic study by the government and by various departments. Although I know the very real difficulties of the problem, I trust that some method will be found of broadening the scope of the act so as to provide for the inclusion of the fishermen. This is a very important matter to us in all parts of the island, for anything which benefits our fishermen benefits all of us.

I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that the measures the government has forecast in the speech from the throne will enable us to meet the problems which this great nation faces, both at home and abroad, with greater strength and a greater chance of success. Finally, I should like to emphasize once again how confident I am that this great country will go on from strength to strength.
On motion of Mr. Croll the debate was adjourned.
